events/1302_esilio/phases/0/prompt: Autumn 1301 · Sent to Rome. The embassy is waiting at the San Piero gate. Take only three things.
events/1302_esilio/phases/0/verdict:
Tried in absence
Exiled for life
Refuses to appear: burn him
events/1302_esilio/phases/1/title: Rome · The pope's audience hall · Autumn 1301
events/1302_esilio/phases/1/narrative: The Blacks want the French king's brother, Charles of Valois, to come and “mediate” in Florence. The city sends three envoys to Rome to plead its case before the pope — Dante is one of them.
events/1302_esilio/phases/1/instruction: Listen carefully in the hall: who is kept, and who is sent away.
events/1302_esilio/phases/1/npcs/0/dialo: Children of Florence, why so anxious? We ask only that your city obey.
The other envoys may go home and carry Our word. This poet — he stays here with Us.
events/1302_esilio/phases/1/npcs/1/dialo: (quietly) Lord Charles of Valois has already marched north with his troops, to “mediate” in Florence.
The Holy Father says: what's your hurry? Stay a few more days.
events/1302_esilio/phases/1/npcs/2/dialo: Mediate? You don't bring a single soldier when you go to mediate.
Keeping me here in Rome… something is about to happen in the city.
events/1302_esilio/phases/2/situation:
The pope sends the other two envoys back to Florence and keeps you alone.
At the same moment, the French king's brother Charles of Valois is marching north with an army — officially, to “mediate.”
events/1302_esilio/phases/2/options/0/te: Charles really does mediate, and both parties give ground
events/1302_esilio/phases/2/options/1/te: The Blacks open the gates to him and the Whites are crushed
events/1302_esilio/phases/2/options/2/te: The Whites hold the city and Charles goes home with nothing
events/1302_esilio/phases/2/sameNote: You guessed it. So you already know what this “mediation” was — now watch it land on you.
events/1302_esilio/phases/2/diffNote: It went the other way. Watch how it happened —
events/1302_esilio/phases/2/consequence:
The Blacks opened the gates for Charles. Corso Donati came back. They burned the Whites' houses and looted the Whites' shops, for six days.
Only then came the trials.
events/1302_esilio/phases/3/title: The road home · Bad news all the way
events/1302_esilio/phases/3/travelNarrat: At last the pope lets him go. On the road home, the news is worse at every stop.
events/1302_esilio/phases/3/instruction: Click each stop along the road.
events/1302_esilio/phases/3/waypoints/0/: “Charles is in the city! He didn't lose a single soldier — the gates opened by themselves.”
events/1302_esilio/phases/3/waypoints/1/: “The Blacks opened the gates for Charles, and Corso Donati is back in the city. They're burning the Whites' houses and looting the Whites' shops.”
events/1302_esilio/phases/3/waypoints/2/: “The new government is trying the Whites without them there… Signor Alighieri — you're on the list.”
events/1302_esilio/phases/4/title: Inn outside the walls · A case on a snowy night
events/1302_esilio/phases/4/narrative: An inn outside Florence. Snow at night. A copy of the sentence is being passed around among the White refugees. What actually happened — put the clues together.
events/1302_esilio/phases/4/instruction: Collect all 5 clues and work out what this trial really was.
events/1302_esilio/phases/4/npcs/0/dialo: “Dante Alighieri: taking bribes, extorting money he had no right to, opposing the pope and Lord Charles — a fine of five thousand florins, two years' exile, and never to hold public office again.”
Bribes? Every account I kept as prior would stand up to inspection. The charge is made up.
events/1302_esilio/phases/4/npcs/1/dialo: Confess and pay by the deadline and they cut the sentence — but confessing means admitting that the Blacks' government is the lawful one.
Confess, and you convict yourself. Refuse, and they get to take your life. Both ways are dead ends.
events/1302_esilio/phases/4/npcs/2/dialo: “The men named above have refused to appear — if any of them falls into the hands of the commune, let him be burned with fire until he dies. (igne comburatur sic quod moriatur)”
The stake. They mean to burn me alive.
events/1302_esilio/phases/4/npcs/3/dialo: Your lady asked me to bring word: “Gemma is staying in the city with the children. She is a Donati daughter — the Blacks will not touch her.”
“Don't come back.” — that was all your lady said.
events/1302_esilio/phases/4/npcs/4/dialo: Fifteen men were sentenced to burn with him on 10 March. Then look at the sentence lists, batch after batch — everyone on them is a leading White. Without exception.
events/1302_esilio/phases/5/narrative: The fire is dying down. Put all the clues together — what was this trial really?
events/1302_esilio/phases/5/options/0/te: I was unlucky. I got caught in a coup.
events/1302_esilio/phases/5/options/0/re: …No. Look again: the timing, the charges, the list. Who is behind all of it?
events/1302_esilio/phases/5/options/1/te: The pope used Charles's sword to purge the Whites — I'm an enemy removed “by law”
events/1302_esilio/phases/5/options/1/re:
Boniface held me in Rome so that Charles's sword could walk in unopposed.
The Blacks held the knife, the French cleared the road, the pope moved the pieces.
The charges were fake, the trial was real — because the trial itself was the weapon.
events/1302_esilio/phases/5/conclusion/n: The charges, the timing, the list — settle on the conclusion first. Next step: prove it.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/claim: This trial was not justice. It was a political purge that used the law as a weapon.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/instruction: Out of what you saw at the inn, pick the 2 things that really support this claim.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/items/0/text: The sentence charges him with “taking bribes and extorting money he had no right to” — but Dante was a prior for two months in all.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/items/0/why: The charge doesn't match the facts, and from first to last not one account book was ever produced. The charge was fitted on afterwards — which means convicting him was never the point.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/items/1/text: The fifteen men sentenced to burn with him on 10 March were all leading Whites, without exception.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/items/1/why: If they were really investigating bribery, the list of the accused would not line up exactly with one party. A list that tidy means people were picked by party, not by crime.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/items/2/text: The second sentence raised the punishment from fine and exile to burning.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/items/2/why: Harsh is not the same as political. A real thief who refuses to appear could have his sentence raised too. This shows they were in a hurry, but on its own it doesn't get you to “purge.”
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/items/3/text: It was snowing in Florence the days the sentence was read out.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/items/3/why: True, but it has nothing to do with the claim. Evidence has to hold the conclusion up. Being true is not enough.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/items/4/text: Gemma stayed in the city with the children and was never touched — she is a Donati daughter.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/items/4/why: This one actually pulls the other way: the Blacks kept family ties, they did not kill every White they saw. True, and important — but it does not support “the trial was a weapon.” Good reasoning means recognizing which facts work against you.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/closing:
Two are enough: the charge, and the list.
The charge doesn't fit, and yet the list covers one party exactly — so what they were handling was not a court case.
events/1302_esilio/phases/7/token/detail: 1302 · Tried in absence, exiled for life, burned if he refuses to appear
events/1302_esilio/phases/7/afterText:
He has an ancestor, speaking in 1300, “foretell” what had already happened in 1302:

“You shall leave behind everything you love most — that is the first arrow the bow of exile shoots.
You shall taste how salty another man's bread is, and how steep another man's stairs are.”

In that same book, he also gave everyone a new place.
events/1302_esilio/phases/8/question: These people — which realm did Dante put each of them in?
events/1302_esilio/phases/8/circles/1/la: Sins that can still be washed clean
events/1302_esilio/phases/8/circles/2/la: Sins that can never be washed clean
events/1302_esilio/phases/8/souls/0/verd: Inferno XIX: in the third ditch of the eighth circle, the men who bought and sold holy office are stuffed head-down into cracks in the rock, with only the soles of their feet left outside to burn. Dante comes to the edge of one hole. Down inside it, Nicholas III mistakes him for someone else and “foretells” that the next man to fill this hole will be Boniface. — When Dante wrote this, Boniface was still alive. He put a living man into Hell, and kept the place ready for him in advance.
events/1302_esilio/phases/8/souls/0/hint: His sin has to do with “money” and “holy office.”
events/1302_esilio/phases/8/souls/1/verd: Head of the Blacks, the man who drove Dante out of the city. Dante does not sentence him with his own hand — he has Corso's own younger brother Forese say it, up in Purgatory: “The one most to blame will be dragged along by a beast, faster and faster, all the way down to the valley where the sin is never washed clean.” (Purgatorio XXIV) Two brothers: one in Purgatory, one below.
events/1302_esilio/phases/8/souls/2/verd: Purgatorio XXIII: the gluttons are so starved that they have lost their shape, and Dante almost fails to recognize his old friend. When they were young the two of them traded insult poems, the really nasty kind. Yet meeting again in Purgatory, they fall into talk as if none of it had happened. — Not everyone he loved is up above, and not everyone who did wrong is down below.
events/1302_esilio/phases/8/souls/2/hint: He is Corso's brother, but he is not Corso.
events/1302_esilio/phases/8/souls/3/metL: 1283 Florence · head of the Santa Trinita bridge
events/1302_esilio/phases/8/souls/3/verd: She appears in Purgatorio XXX, takes Dante over from Virgil, and leads him all the way to the final light of Paradiso XXXIII. The girl in the crimson dress at that party, when he was nine years old, ends up as the guide for the whole poem.
events/1302_esilio/phases/8/souls/3/hint: She is the one who leads the way.
events/1302_esilio/phases/9/transitionTe: Boccaccio puts down his lecture notes.
events/1302_esilio/phases/9/dufu_reactio:
The man you just put into Hell was talking to you in Rome a quarter of an hour ago.

That is how this book was made. He did not invent a Hell —
he took Florence, and Rome, and everyone he knew in his life,
and seated them all over again, level by level.
quiz/1302_esilio/quizzes/0/question: What was Dante charged with at the 1302 trial held without him?
quiz/1302_esilio/quizzes/0/options/1: Taking bribes (the charge was made up)
quiz/1302_esilio/quizzes/0/options/3: Refusing to serve as a soldier
quiz/1302_esilio/quizzes/0/explanation: The sentence of 27 January 1302 fined him and sent him into exile for “taking bribes and extorting money he had no right to” — and no evidence was ever produced. It was a political purge: Pope Boniface VIII used Charles of Valois's sword, and the Blacks carried it out.
quiz/1302_esilio/quizzes/1/question: The second sentence, on 10 March 1302, said that if Florence caught Dante he would be punished how?
quiz/1302_esilio/quizzes/1/explanation: The second sentence says it in so many words: “if he falls into the hands of the commune, let him be burned with fire until he dies” (igne comburatur sic quod moriatur). Beheading was the changed sentence, after he refused the amnesty in 1315.
quiz/1302_esilio/quizzes/2/question:
Paradiso XVII: his ancestor Cacciaguida foretells the exile.
“You shall taste how ___ another man's bread is, and how steep another man's stairs are”
quiz/1302_esilio/quizzes/2/explanation: The exile prophecy in Paradiso XVII is one of the most famous passages in the Divine Comedy — “come sa di sale lo pane altrui.” The writing turns time around: Dante, already in exile, has his ancestor “foretell” to his 1300 self everything that has already happened.
cast/people/boniface/life/0: Trained as a scholar of Church law. Worked as a diplomat for the papal court.
cast/people/boniface/life/1: Elected pope in 1294. The pope before him, Celestine V, had stepped down on his own — and at the time there were people in Rome who said Boniface had talked him into it.
cast/people/boniface/life/2: In 1300 he held the first “Jubilee” in Christian history: anyone who came to Rome as a pilgrim was forgiven their sins. People poured into the city from all over Europe. The offerings piled up on the altar of St. Peter's like little hills, and priests stood there raking them in.
cast/people/boniface/life/3: In 1302 he issued Unam Sanctam: anyone who does not obey the pope in Rome cannot be saved. It was the highest claim papal power ever made.
cast/people/boniface/life/4: In 1303, at Anagni, men of King Philip IV of France seized him and humiliated him for three days. A month after they let him go, he died in Rome.
cast/people/boniface/withDante/0: In the autumn of 1301, Florence sent three envoys to Rome to plead its case, and Dante was one of them. He sent the other two home and kept Dante behind.
cast/people/boniface/withDante/1: At the same time, he let Charles of Valois, the French king's brother, march north with troops to “mediate” in Florence. The city opened its own gates. Then came the Blacks' coup, six days of burning and looting, and then that trial.
cast/people/corso_donati/role: Leader of the Blacks, old Florentine noble
cast/people/corso_donati/life/0: Eldest son of the Donati family. Served as chief magistrate of Bologna and of Pistoia.
cast/people/corso_donati/life/1: At Campaldino in 1289 he charged with his cavalry against orders, and won — the credit went on his record, and so did the disobedience.
cast/people/corso_donati/life/2: In 1300 the priors banished him (Dante was one of the priors who signed).
cast/people/corso_donati/life/3: In November 1301 he came back into the city with Charles of Valois and tore the Whites out by the roots. For the next few years he was the man who really ran Florence.
cast/people/corso_donati/life/4: In 1308 his own Blacks accused him of treason. He rode off to escape, Catalan mercenaries caught up with him, and he died on the road outside the city.
cast/people/corso_donati/withDante/0: Dante's wife Gemma was a Donati too — they counted as distant relatives.
cast/people/corso_donati/withDante/1: During the two months Dante was a prior in 1300, his name was on the banishment list. A year later he was back, and the name on the list was Dante's.
cast/people/forese/role: Dante's boyhood friend, Corso's younger brother
cast/people/forese/life/0: Corso's younger brother, Piccarda's older brother. Three of them in one family, and not alike at all.
cast/people/forese/life/1: He never did anything big. He ate too much, loved a good time, and was always short of money.
cast/people/forese/life/2: He died in 1296, six years before Dante's exile — he never saw the great upheaval.
cast/people/forese/withDante/0: When they were young the two of them traded a whole round of insult poems, the really nasty kind: your family is poor, your wife, your coughing in the middle of the night. A set like that is called a tenzone. Both of them kept the poems. Neither destroyed them.
cast/people/forese/withDante/1: When he died, Dante was still in Florence and had not yet gone into politics.
cast/people/beatrice_young/life/0: Her father, Folco Portinari, was one of Florence's great bankers. He paid for the building of the hospital of Santa Maria Nuova.
cast/people/beatrice_young/life/1: She married Simone de' Bardi, of a banking family.
cast/people/beatrice_young/life/2: She died in June 1290, twenty-four years old.
cast/people/beatrice_young/withDante/0: In 1274, when he was nine, he saw her for the first time at a party at her house. She was wearing a crimson dress.
cast/people/beatrice_young/withDante/1: In 1283, when they were both eighteen, she greeted him at the head of the Santa Trinita bridge — Dante wrote: in that moment I seemed to see the very limit of happiness.
cast/people/beatrice_young/withDante/2: In their whole lives they said no more than a few words to each other. After she died, he made a vow at the end of the Vita Nuova: to write about her what no one had ever written about any woman.
cast/people/brunetto/role: Notary, chancellor of the commune, teacher of Florence
cast/people/brunetto/life/0: A Guelph. After the defeat at Montaperti in 1260 he spent six years in exile in France.
cast/people/brunetto/life/1: In France, in French, he wrote the big book of his life, the Trésor — an encyclopedia meant to hold all the learning in the world. His reason: French goes further, more people read it.
cast/people/brunetto/life/2: He also wrote a much shorter verse book in everyday Italian, the Tesoretto. In it the author loses his way in a wood, meets a goddess, and is led on a tour of the reasons behind all things.
cast/people/brunetto/life/3: He came back to the city in 1266 and rose to chancellor of the commune. Villani said he was the one who took the Florentines “from rough to fine” — who taught the city how to speak and how to argue politics.
cast/people/brunetto/withDante/0: We do not actually know how they met: no school record, no contract, not one letter.
cast/people/brunetto/withDante/1: We know there was such a teacher only because Dante later wrote about him.
cast/people/brunetto/withDante/2: What he taught was rhetoric and politics — how to make a whole city understand you. And one line Dante remembered all his life: a man can make himself immortal.
cast/people/piccarda/role: A nun, younger sister of Corso and Forese
cast/people/piccarda/life/0: The youngest child of the Donati family. Corso's sister, Forese's sister.
cast/people/piccarda/life/1: She entered the order of Saint Clare as a nun and took vows for life.
cast/people/piccarda/life/2: For the sake of a political marriage, her brother Corso brought men into the convent, dragged her out, and forced her to marry.
cast/people/piccarda/life/3: She fell ill and died not long after the wedding. Some say she wanted to die — her vow was broken, and she would not go on living with that.
cast/people/piccarda/withDante/0: Dante's wife Gemma was a Donati too, and the two families saw a great deal of each other.
cast/people/piccarda/withDante/1: He knew both her brothers: one was the friend he traded insults with when they were young, the other was the man who drove him out of Florence.
cast/people/cacciaguida/life/0: Born in the old Florence, when the walls were still small. People dressed plainly then, and girls marrying did not compete over dowries.
cast/people/cacciaguida/life/1: He married a woman from the Po valley whose family name was Alighieri — the name was passed down from there, and a hundred years and more later it came to Dante.
cast/people/cacciaguida/life/2: He followed the Emperor Conrad III on the Second Crusade and died fighting in the Holy Land.
cast/people/cacciaguida/withDante/0: He is Dante's great-great-grandfather, four generations back.
cast/people/cacciaguida/withDante/1: In the Paradiso, Dante claims him as his ancestor and has him tell of the old Florence — and say that line about exile: how salty another man's bread is, how steep another man's stairs are.
timeline/character/description: Author of the Divine Comedy, the first sign of the European Renaissance, “father of the Italian language”
timeline/stages/0/summary: Dante was born into a minor noble family in Florence. At nine he first saw Beatrice; as a young man he wrote the Vita Nuova. After she died, he turned to books and to a teacher.
timeline/stages/0/events/0/summary: Under the sign of Gemini, a son is born to the Alighieri. The old Florence of his ancestor Cacciaguida — and the first spark of the two parties' quarrel.
timeline/stages/0/events/1/summary: The greeting at the bridge, the battlefield of Campaldino, the death bell of 1290 — and the vow in the last chapter of the Vita Nuova.
timeline/stages/0/events/2/summary: After Beatrice died, he buried himself in books. The most learned old man in the city taught him rhetoric, politics, and one line he did not understand yet.
timeline/stages/0/events/2/comedyAnchor/: Sand under rain of fire · his teacher again
timeline/stages/1/summary: Dante joined the guild of doctors and apothecaries and stepped into politics. He became a prior — and with his own hand banished his closest friend.
timeline/stages/1/events/0/summary: Under the Ordinances of Justice, the poet joins the guild of doctors and apothecaries to win the right to take part in government. Under the surface, the Whites and the Blacks are already stirring.
timeline/stages/1/events/1/summary: Rome in its Jubilee year, Florence with Dante as prior; on the banishment list is his best friend's name. The Divine Comedy is set in this year.
timeline/stages/1/events/1/comedyAnchor/: Old Cavalcanti: where is my son?
timeline/stages/2/summary: Tried in his absence, banished for life, sentenced to burn. Under other men's roofs, Dante began to write the Divine Comedy.
timeline/stages/2/events/0/summary: The pope holds the envoy, the Blacks seize the city, the trial goes on without him: a fine, exile, and burning if he will not confess. He never set foot in Florence again.
timeline/stages/2/events/0/comedyAnchor/: Another man's bread · the pope planted upside down
timeline/stages/2/events/1/summary: The shame of eating at a great lord's table, the break with the exiled Whites; the choice to write in the everyday tongue, and the words over the gate of Hell.
timeline/stages/2/events/1/comedyAnchor/: The words over the gate of Hell
timeline/stages/2/events/2/summary: Henry VII comes south, and Dante writes open letter after open letter, staking everything. In 1313, at Buonconvento, the emperor falls suddenly ill and dies. The dream breaks.
timeline/stages/2/events/2/comedyAnchor/: The empty seat kept for Henry
timeline/stages/2/events/3/summary: Pay the fine, put on the penitent's robe, walk through the streets to the Baptistery — and he could go home. He refused: “Home by that road? Never.”
timeline/stages/2/events/3/comedyAnchor/: If ever this sacred poem brings me home
timeline/stages/3/summary: Guido Novello's welcome, his children around him again, the Paradiso finished. In September 1321 the poet was laid to rest in Ravenna.
timeline/stages/3/events/0/summary: Pine woods and golden mosaics, the test by three apostles, the fever caught on the way back from Venice, and the tale of the thirteen lost cantos.
events/1265_firenze/phases/0/narrative: 1373, Florence, the church of Santo Stefano. The first “Dante lectures” in history begin — the speaker: Giovanni Boccaccio.
events/1265_firenze/phases/0/instruction: Click Boccaccio at the lectern and hear him begin.
events/1265_firenze/phases/0/npcs/0/dial: In 1265, under the sign of Gemini, a baby was born in this city.
Fifty years later, the same city sentenced him to burn.
Today the city pays me to talk about him. My friends — let's start at the beginning.
events/1265_firenze/phases/1/title: Outside the Baptistery of San Giovanni
events/1265_firenze/phases/1/narrative: May 1265, Florence. A son is born to the Alighieri. They name him Durante — for short, Dante.
events/1265_firenze/phases/1/instruction: Walk around the market outside the Baptistery and hear what the city is saying.
events/1265_firenze/phases/1/npcs/0/dial: Here a guild's banner counts for more than a lord's sword. That's Florence.
Wool cloth, banks, spices — we live on trade, not on castles.
events/1265_firenze/phases/1/npcs/1/dial: Five years ago, Montaperti. The Ghibellines came back at us with Siena's troops…
The water of the Arbia ran red.
The emperor's party, the pope's party — a child born in this city has to pick a side.
events/1265_firenze/phases/1/npcs/2/dial: The Alighieri? Minor nobles, Guelphs — that's the pope's party.
They say that while she was carrying him, his mother dreamed she gave birth under a laurel tree.
events/1265_firenze/phases/1/npcs/3/dial: See that eight-sided baptistery? San Giovanni — our “beautiful St John.”
The font inside — every child in this city starts there.
events/1265_firenze/phases/1/npcs/4/dial: The eight-sided Baptistery stands in the middle of the square, its marble walls bright in the morning light. Next spring, on Holy Saturday, the baby called Dante will be baptised here along with all the city's newborns.
events/1265_firenze/phases/2/prompt: His great-great-grandfather is telling his own life. Put it back in order.
events/1265_firenze/phases/2/panels/1/ca: A woman at her spindle, telling stories
events/1265_firenze/phases/2/panels/2/ca: A wife from the Po valley
events/1265_firenze/phases/2/panels/3/ca: He rides off under the cross
events/1265_firenze/phases/2/revealNote:
A city, a household, a marriage, a crusade — and it all lands on one baby.
He isn't telling history. He's telling where this child comes from.
events/1265_firenze/phases/3/narrative: At the lectern, Boccaccio opens Paradiso XV — Dante's great-great-grandfather Cacciaguida, the crusader martyr, remembering the old, plain Florence.
events/1265_firenze/phases/3/instruction: Click the picture and go panel by panel.
events/1265_firenze/phases/3/panels/0/di: “Florence, inside her old walls, lived plain and quiet. The bells rang for morning and midday prayer, the way they always had.”
events/1265_firenze/phases/3/panels/1/di: “The mothers kept to spindle and thread, and by the cradle told the old stories — Troy, Fiesole and Rome.”
events/1265_firenze/phases/3/panels/2/di: “My wife came from the Po valley. Your family name — Alighieri — came from her.”
events/1265_firenze/phases/3/panels/3/di: “Then I followed the Emperor Conrad on crusade, and died for the faith in the Holy Land. From that death I came to this peace.”
events/1265_firenze/phases/3/panels/4/di: Holy Saturday, the next spring. The baby is baptised in the Baptistery of San Giovanni and named Durante Alighieri.
“Out of my blood will come a man who walks through all three realms.”
events/1265_firenze/phases/4/narrative: Nine years pass. The Alighieri boy grows up among parchment and copied books. His mother died young; his father makes a small living lending money.
events/1265_firenze/phases/4/instruction: Click the things in the study, and the family.
events/1265_firenze/phases/4/npcs/0/dial: A copy of the Aeneid lies open on the desk — the epic of Virgil of Mantua. The margins are covered in a boy's clumsy notes.
This man from Mantua… my teacher.
events/1265_firenze/phases/4/npcs/1/dial: A dusty spindle stands in the corner. His mother Bella died when he was small.
…Was the dream under the laurel tree true, mother?
events/1265_firenze/phases/4/npcs/2/dial: Reading again? Fine. For a small house like ours, the pen is safer than the sword.
There's a feast tomorrow at a great house. You're coming with me. Wear something decent.
events/1265_firenze/phases/5/transitionT:
In May of his ninth year, at a feast, he saw a girl in a crimson dress.
Later he wrote:
“Behold, a god stronger than I, who comes to rule over me.”
events/1265_firenze/phases/5/announcemen: Boccaccio: “My friends, remember that crimson dress. What a nine-year-old felt that day will grow into the biggest poem in the Christian world.”
quiz/1265_firenze/quizzes/0/question: In the Florence where Dante was born, which two parties made the deepest political split?
quiz/1265_firenze/quizzes/0/options/1: The Guelphs (the pope's party) and the Ghibellines (the emperor's party)
quiz/1265_firenze/quizzes/0/explanation: In the 13th century Italy was split between the Guelphs, who backed the pope, and the Ghibellines, who backed the Holy Roman Emperor. At Montaperti in 1260 the Ghibellines used Siena's army to crush Florence's Guelphs. The Whites and the Blacks came later — a split inside the Guelphs themselves.
quiz/1265_firenze/quizzes/1/question: In Paradiso XV, which ancestor tells Dante about the “old, plain Florence”?
quiz/1265_firenze/quizzes/1/explanation: Cacciaguida is Dante's great-great-grandfather. He went on the Second Crusade with the Emperor Conrad III and died fighting. In Paradiso XV–XVII he remembers the old city and foretells Dante's exile. The name Alighieri came from his wife.
quiz/1265_firenze/quizzes/2/question:
After nine-year-old Dante first saw Beatrice, he wrote:
“Behold, a god ___ than I, who comes to rule over me”
quiz/1265_firenze/quizzes/2/explanation: From chapter two of the Vita Nuova. At a feast, nine-year-old Dante saw Beatrice for the first time, and from then on “the god of love ruled my soul” — and that feeling grew, in the end, into the Divine Comedy.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/0/transition: At the lectern, Boccaccio opens the Vita Nuova.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/0/announceme: Boccaccio: “In his whole life he spoke to her only a few times. She married a banker. He married a wife chosen for politics. Yet in the Divine Comedy the one who leads him up to Heaven is not his wife — it is her. How did that happen?”
events/1283_beatrice/phases/1/narrative: Eighteen years old. The Arno in the morning light. A woman in white comes across the bridge with two companions.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/1/instructio: Click the people at the bridge, and write this moment down.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/1/npcs/0/dia: She crosses the bridge, turns her face toward him, and gives him a small nod.
In that moment I seemed to see the very limit of happiness.
Her greeting had a gentleness in it I have no words for. I was dazed. I ran back to my room like a man escaping a crowd, and began to think about her.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/1/npcs/1/dia: Off in a daze again? Write it down, Durante.
What we write is the “sweet new style” — love is not a knight's prize. It is the thing that makes a soul noble.
When it's written, bring it to me. You call me your first friend — don't hand me some ordinary sonnet.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/1/npcs/2/dia: That is Bice of the Portinari — already promised to one of the Bardi.
Every poet in the city is writing about her. She just goes on greeting everyone kindly, the way she always has.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/2/transition:
June 1289, Campaldino. Dante, twenty-four, rode in the front rank of the light cavalry and fought all day.
Afterwards he almost never spoke of that battle.

The war was over.
But the next summer the funeral bells of Florence
rang for a woman of twenty-four.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/3/title: The City Has Become a Widow
events/1283_beatrice/phases/3/panels/0/d: The bridge is empty. That gentle greeting will never come again.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/3/panels/1/d: A funeral procession in white carries white flowers through the whole city.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/3/panels/2/d: In the Vita Nuova he mourns her with a line out of Lamentations — the way you mourn a holy city that has fallen.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/4/title: The End of the Vita Nuova
events/1283_beatrice/phases/4/narrative: After the grief, the Vita Nuova needs an ending.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/4/question: After the grief, what will you write for her?
events/1283_beatrice/phases/4/options/0/: Write every last lament, then forget her
You won't forget. We both know that.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/4/options/1/: Write nothing more of her — until I can “write of her as no one ever has”

Until I am worthy of her, I put down my pen.
If Heaven grants me the years, I will write of her what has never been written of any woman.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/4/conclusion: The Vita Nuova ends there. He really did stop. The vow waited twenty years — waited until he had lost everything — before it was kept, at a length of more than fourteen thousand lines. And the keeping of it starts with her, waiting for him at the top of the mountain of Purgatory: “Look at me well. I am, I truly am, Beatrice.”
events/1283_beatrice/phases/5/transition: At the lectern, Boccaccio lays the last chapter of the Vita Nuova side by side with Purgatorio XXX.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/5/announceme: Boccaccio: “Gentlemen — she is not his ‘girlfriend.’ She is a god he built for himself. Understand that, and you have found the door of the Comedy.”
quiz/1283_beatrice/quizzes/0/question: Which battle did Dante fight in as a light cavalryman in 1289?
quiz/1283_beatrice/quizzes/0/explanation: In 1289 Florence met Arezzo on the plain of Campaldino. Dante was in it, in the front rank of the light cavalry, and said later that he felt “very great fear, and in the end very great joy.” Montaperti (1260) was before he was born; Lastra (1304) was a crushing defeat for the exiled Whites.
quiz/1283_beatrice/quizzes/1/question: After Beatrice died, what did Dante vow at the end of the Vita Nuova?
quiz/1283_beatrice/quizzes/1/options/0: To write every lament for her, then let her go
quiz/1283_beatrice/quizzes/1/options/1: Never to marry, and to enter a monastery
quiz/1283_beatrice/quizzes/1/options/2: To write nothing more of her, until he could write of her as no one ever has
quiz/1283_beatrice/quizzes/1/options/3: To build a chapel for her
quiz/1283_beatrice/quizzes/1/explanation: The last chapter of the Vita Nuova: Dante puts down his pen until he can “write of her what has never been written of any woman.” Twenty years later the Comedy keeps that vow — she becomes the guide who leads him up to Heaven.
quiz/1283_beatrice/quizzes/2/question:
Purgatorio XXX. She appears at the top of the mountain of Purgatory and says:
“Look at me well. I am, I truly am, ___”
quiz/1283_beatrice/quizzes/2/explanation: Purgatorio XXX: Virgil slips away without a word, and Beatrice arrives — “Guardaci ben! Ben son, ben son Beatrice.” They parted at the bridge; they meet again at the top of the mountain of Purgatory. The vow of the Vita Nuova is kept here.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/0/transition: Boccaccio turns a page and stops.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/0/announceme:
We don't actually know how Dante came to know Brunetto Latini. No school record, no contract, not one letter.
There is only one reason we know of this teacher at all — Dante wrote him into the Inferno.
Hold on to that: the evidence for the real half comes from the literary half.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/0/dufu_react:
So today's lesson runs backwards.
First see how the two of them got on in this world — then see where the student put his teacher.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/1/narrative: Two years after Beatrice died. Dante is twenty-seven and has buried himself in books. The most learned old man in the city is Brunetto Latini — notary, former chancellor of the commune, the man who taught this city how to speak and how to argue politics.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/1/instructio: Talk with the teacher. Look at the two books on his desk.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/1/npcs/0/dia: Writing poems is no great skill, boy. This city has more men who write poems than men who read them.
The skill is this: making a whole city understand you. Rhetoric is not decoration, it is politics. If you want to go into politics, first learn how to get your words inside other people's hearts.

A man's life is short. But a man can make himself immortal — by leaving behind something that outlives him.
You don't understand me yet. You will.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/1/npcs/1/dia: The Trésor · Li Livres dou Trésor
The big book of the teacher's life: an encyclopedia meant to hold all the learning in the world. Astronomy, history, ethics, rhetoric, how to govern a city — all of it.
After Montaperti I was exiled to France. I wrote it in those six years. French goes further, more people read it. Learning that can't travel isn't learning.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/1/npcs/2/dia: Beside it, a thin one: verse in everyday Italian. In the poem the author loses his way in a wood, meets a goddess, and is led on a tour of the reasons behind all things.
…Lost in a wood. Led along by someone.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/1/npcs/3/dia: The master is old now. You've come late — he's been back from France nearly thirty years.
The whole city has been taught by him. They say he's the one who took the Florentines “from rough to fine.”
events/1292_brunetto/phases/2/narrative: The teacher's big book is in French, his small one in the everyday tongue. One day Dante will have to choose too.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/2/question: To write a book that outlives you, which language should you use?
events/1292_brunetto/phases/2/options/0/: the scholars' language, the respectable one
Respectable. But your mother can't read it. Your neighbour can't read it. Who are you writing for?
events/1292_brunetto/phases/2/options/1/: like your teacher did — it travels further

That is what I chose. More people do read it.
…Only, it isn't the language I was born speaking.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/2/options/2/: the way people talk in the streets of Florence

If a thing is to outlive me, it has to be written in a living language.
Latin is dead. French is not mine.
I will write a book anyone can read, in the language my mother taught me.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/2/conclusion:
In 1292 this choice is still only talk. A dozen years later a penniless man in exile will use it to write a long poem in interlocking three-line rhyme — in the “everyday tongue,” not in any respectable language. That poem went on to turn that “everyday tongue” into Italian.
His teacher chose the other road.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/3/token/deta: 1292 · Brunetto Latini, who taught him rhetoric, politics, and “how a man makes himself immortal”
events/1292_brunetto/phases/3/afterText:
Seventh circle, third ring.
Fire falls like rain on the sand, and has fallen forever.
A band of souls comes along the bank, squinting up at him.
One of them suddenly catches him by the hem.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/4/recognitio:
The fire has scorched the face past recognising.
Dante bends down and stares a long time before he knows him —

“Are you here, Ser Brunetto?”
events/1292_brunetto/phases/4/asks/0/q: You look up to him. Why is he here?
events/1292_brunetto/phases/4/asks/0/a:
Because respect does not cancel the sin.
I sentenced him to the ring for sins “against nature.” It is the hardest passage in the whole book to write.
If I moved a man somewhere he doesn't belong just because I loved him —
then this whole Hell is worth nothing.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/4/asks/1/q: Then why do you still address him as “voi,” the respectful you?
events/1292_brunetto/phases/4/asks/1/a:
In the whole book there are fewer than five souls I say “voi” to.
I am the one who sentenced him and I am the one who honours him. I don't intend to make those two agree.
You heard that line just now — “you taught me how a man makes himself immortal.”
That is not politeness. That is what I owe him.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/4/asks/2/q: What did he say for himself?
events/1292_brunetto/phases/4/asks/2/a:
Not one word in his own defence.
He asked for one thing only: his Trésor.
“Let my Trésor be left in your care — in that book I am still alive.”
Then he ran off. Like the men racing for the green cloth at Verona —
and he still looked like the one who wins, not the one who loses.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/4/asks/3/q: Writing him in here — is that punishing him, or saving him?
events/1292_brunetto/phases/4/asks/3/a:
Decide for yourself.
Seven hundred years have gone by. People remember Brunetto Latini,
not because of that Trésor in French —
but because I put him under the rain of fire.
The “immortality” he wanted, I gave him. This is how.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/4/closing:
He taught Dante how a man makes himself immortal.
Dante did it — and took his teacher in with him.

A real teacher became a soul in Inferno XV.
That is how the Divine Comedy was built: he put the people he knew into it, one by one.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/5/quote:
“If you follow your star, you cannot fail to reach a glorious harbour…
But that ungrateful, spiteful people will turn against you for the good you do.
Keep clear of them.”
events/1292_brunetto/phases/5/instructio: Don't read on yet. Put each of these three times where it belongs.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/5/axis/0/lab:
Brunetto says this
(time inside the story)
events/1292_brunetto/phases/5/axis/2/lab:
Dante writes the passage
(the author's time)
events/1292_brunetto/phases/5/blocks/1/t:
January 1302
Tried in absence, exiled for life
events/1292_brunetto/phases/5/blocks/2/t:
Sometime in the 1310s
In exile, under other men's roofs
events/1292_brunetto/phases/5/question: So is this a prophecy, or a memory?
events/1292_brunetto/phases/5/conclusion:
Brunetto thinks he is talking about the future.
By the time Dante wrote it, that “future” was more than ten years past.

He has a man in his book “foretell” suffering he had already been through.
So every prophecy in the Comedy is doubled:
the character looks forward, the author looks back, and the two lines of sight collide at the year 1300.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/6/transition: At the lectern, Boccaccio closes Canto XV.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/6/dufu_react:
For six hundred years scholars have argued about one thing:
what sin “against nature” did Brunetto actually commit?
Some say a sin of the body. Others say —
he turned his back on his own mother tongue and wrote the book of his life in French.

Which answer is right, we don't know.
But notice this: the man who sentenced him is exactly the man who decided to write in his mother tongue.
quiz/1292_brunetto/quizzes/0/question: The Trésor, the big book of Brunetto Latini's life — what language was it written in?
quiz/1292_brunetto/quizzes/0/explanation: After the defeat at Montaperti, Brunetto went into exile in France, and there wrote the encyclopedic Trésor in French — his reason was that French goes further. He also wrote a verse book in everyday Italian, the Tesoretto, but a much slighter one. That choice later became one of the keys to reading Inferno XV.
quiz/1292_brunetto/quizzes/1/question: When Dante meets Brunetto again in the Inferno, he does something he does for only a handful of souls in the whole book. What?
quiz/1292_brunetto/quizzes/1/options/3: Pulls him out of the rain of fire
quiz/1292_brunetto/quizzes/1/explanation: In the whole poem there are no more than five souls Dante addresses with the respectful voi. He sentenced his teacher to Hell and still spoke to him with the respectful form — the verdict and the respect hold at the same time, and that is the hardest thing about this canto.
quiz/1292_brunetto/quizzes/2/question:
Inferno XV, what Dante says to his teacher:
“You taught me how a man makes himself ___”
quiz/1292_brunetto/quizzes/2/explanation: “m'insegnavate come l'uom s'etterna” — you taught me how a man makes himself immortal. Brunetto taught him that; and the way Dante made his teacher immortal was to write him into the seventh circle, under the rain of fire.
events/1295_arte/phases/0/transitionText: At the lectern, Boccaccio closes the Vita Nuova and takes up a volume of city records.
events/1295_arte/phases/0/announcement/t: Boccaccio: “If you want to destroy a poet, first put him into politics. In 1295 he went and signed up with a guild — the guild of doctors and apothecaries. Don't laugh: in those days books were filed with the medicines.”
events/1295_arte/phases/1/narrative: The Ordinances of Justice are in force: the great families may hold no office, and anyone who wants a say in the city must join a guild. Dante, thirty years old, walks in among the medicine drawers and the scales, to sign one piece of paper that will change his life.
events/1295_arte/phases/1/instruction: Sign the register, and listen to Florence's new quarrel while you're there.
events/1295_arte/phases/1/npcs/0/dialogu: You know the new Ordinances of Justice? They're aimed at the great families and their bullying — a commoner who wants office has to join a guild.
Entered in the guild of doctors and apothecaries, year's dues paid. Congratulations — you can take part in government now.
events/1295_arte/phases/1/npcs/1/dialogu: A poet? You belong to us.
Don't pull that face — spices, medicines, pigments, books: all of them rare goods from far away, all carried in along the same road.
events/1295_arte/phases/1/npcs/2/dialogu: A new copy of Virgil, come up from Bologna. Want it? I'll give you a good price.
More people can read now. Florence's arithmetic schools are busier than the monasteries. Books are good business.
events/1295_arte/phases/1/npcs/3/dialogu: Lord Corso of the Donati was out in the square shouting at people again this morning — his lot are called the Blacks now.
The Cerchi made their money in trade — rich, new money. Their lot are called the Whites. Both of them Guelphs, and they go at each other like dogs.
The Ghibellines — the emperor's side? Driven out of the city long ago. The whole city is Guelph now, the pope's side. No enemy left outside, so they fight their own.
events/1295_arte/phases/2/narrative: The paperwork is done. On the Ponte Vecchio in the last light, the others are waiting for him.
events/1295_arte/phases/2/instruction: Talk to your friends on the bridge, then listen to your own heart.
events/1295_arte/phases/2/npcs/0/dialogu: Politics is mud, Durante. You and I write poems.
(The Guido saying this is himself a leading man of the Whites.)
events/1295_arte/phases/2/npcs/1/dialogu: Well now, “my lord”! A great man of the apothecaries' guild! Do I get a discount on my medicine from here on?
We'll trade a few more sonnets soon — I still owe you an answer for that last one you wrote at me.
(Forese is Corso's younger brother, and Dante's drinking companion. The two of them wrote rude poems at each other, every line drawing blood — and the friendship was real too.)
events/1295_arte/phases/2/npcs/2/dialogu: Guido says politics is mud. And yet—
A city should have order, the way a poem does. I'm going to go and write that order into it.
events/1295_arte/phases/3/lede:
You are the head of one Florentine family. The family across from you is not of your party.
Every time the city changes hands, whoever is in power has to decide: drive the other side out, or let them stay.
The ones you drive out do not disappear — they wait in another city, waiting to come back with outside help.
events/1295_arte/phases/3/coda/lines/0: In 1300 Dante signed a list of men to be banished. His best friend's name was on it.
events/1295_arte/phases/3/coda/lines/1: When he signed it he believed this: hold both parties to the same rule, and the city will settle down.
events/1295_arte/phases/3/coda/lines/2: In 1302 that same rule drove him out.
events/1295_arte/phases/3/coda/lines/3: In 1315 Florence said: pay the fine, put on the penitent's robe, walk through the streets to the Baptistery, and you can come home. He refused.
events/1295_arte/phases/3/coda/lines/4: What was wrong with Florence was never that one side was worse than the other. It was that the city turned “exile” into a move you could play over and over —
events/1295_arte/phases/3/coda/lines/5: the loser can always come back with outside help, and the winner knows it, so each time he strikes harder.
events/1295_arte/phases/3/coda/turn:
Then he wrote the Inferno.
A world with only one round: once the sentence is given it never changes, there is no next move, no way back.

And the lowest level of Hell is not for killing, not for violence —
it is for betrayal. For the people who destroy trust.
That level is frozen: down there, nothing will ever change again.
events/1295_arte/phases/4/transitionText: A different voice takes the lectern — Pietro Alighieri, Dante's son, one of the first men to write a commentary on the Divine Comedy.
events/1295_arte/phases/4/announcement/t: Echoes down the years · Pietro's commentary

“My father believed a city could be governed by reason. Later, in Inferno VI, he has Ciacco the glutton foretell how this city would tear itself apart — the two parties at each other, blood in the streets. That prophecy is really a memory. And through Ciacco's mouth he names the disease: pride, envy and greed are the three sparks that set every heart burning.”
quiz/1295_arte/quizzes/0/question: In 1295, which guild did Dante join in order to take part in government?
quiz/1295_arte/quizzes/0/options/0: The guild of doctors and apothecaries
quiz/1295_arte/quizzes/0/explanation: Under the Ordinances of Justice, you had to belong to a guild to take part in government. Books were classed with medicines then, and booksellers hung on to the apothecaries' guild — so the poet signed up with the doctors and apothecaries.
quiz/1295_arte/quizzes/1/question: In the 1290s the Guelphs of Florence split into the Whites and the Blacks. Which family led each?
quiz/1295_arte/quizzes/1/explanation: The Whites were led by the Cerchi, new money grown rich in trade; the Blacks by Corso of the Donati, an old noble house. Both were Guelphs, and they fought each other to the death — Dante's family were Whites.
quiz/1295_arte/quizzes/2/question:
Inferno VI: Ciacco foretells how Florence will tear itself apart.
“Pride, envy and greed are the three ___ that set every heart burning”
quiz/1295_arte/quizzes/2/explanation: Inferno VI: Ciacco foretells to Dante that the two parties will fight and the Whites will be driven out — and he names the disease: “pride, envy and greed are the three sparks that set every heart burning.”
events/1300_priore/phases/0/transitionTe: At the lectern, Boccaccio writes down a year: 1300.
events/1300_priore/phases/0/announcement: Boccaccio: “Remember this year. In real life, this is the year he became a prior. And he set the story of the Divine Comedy in this year too — the middle of a life. Why? Listen, and you will see.”
events/1300_priore/phases/1/travelNarrat: Pope Boniface VIII invents the “Jubilee”: anyone who comes to Rome as a pilgrim this year has every sin forgiven. Two hundred thousand people pour into Rome — Dante among them.
events/1300_priore/phases/1/instruction: Click each stop along the route.
events/1300_priore/phases/1/waypoints/0/: The whole city is packing. To Rome! To the Jubilee!
events/1300_priore/phases/1/waypoints/1/: The old road never empties: pilgrims, peddlers, beggars, a lady's litter. Every language is saying the same word — Rome.
events/1300_priore/phases/1/waypoints/2/: Inside the gates and out, people swarm like ants. On the bridge the crowd is split into two lines going opposite ways, so nobody gets trampled.
Like an army crossing a bridge, in two lines… I am keeping this picture.
events/1300_priore/phases/2/narrative: Rome. Two hundred thousand pilgrims turn the streets into rivers.
events/1300_priore/phases/2/instruction: Click the people and things in the scene.
events/1300_priore/phases/2/npcs/0/dialo: Guards keeping order have split the bridge down the middle: one side for those going to St Peter's, the other for those coming back.
Years later I wrote the ditches of Hell's eighth circle: the sinners walk in two lines, opposite ways — “just like the crowd on the bridge in Rome in the Jubilee year.”
events/1300_priore/phases/2/npcs/1/dialo: Hymns in every accent, all mixed together. Some have come the whole way on their knees, and their knees are raw.
events/1300_priore/phases/2/npcs/2/name: The money chest by the altar
events/1300_priore/phases/2/npcs/2/dialo: By the altar, priests rake a mountain of offerings into the chest with long rakes, day and night.
Forgiveness and gold coin, traded across the same altar.
events/1300_priore/phases/3/transitionTe:
Outside St Peter's. Far off on a high platform, a figure in a gold crown takes the cheers of two hundred thousand people.
No conversation. Only power, pressing down.
events/1300_priore/phases/3/announcement: Boniface VIII: “Whoever comes devoutly to the tomb of the Apostle in this holy year shall have every sin forgiven.”
events/1300_priore/phases/3/dufu_reactio: He has taken the keys of Heaven and cast them into a sceptre for this world. Remember this man — Boniface.
events/1300_priore/phases/4/petitions/0/: “You'd drive us out too? We're your own party.”
“Then I'll go to the pope myself.”
events/1300_priore/phases/4/petitions/1/: Leave me out of it. I'm your best friend.
events/1300_priore/phases/4/petitions/2/: Exile both sides together. That is the only way the rule holds.
“Why are we counted in as well?”
“Then what have we been doing these two months?”
events/1300_priore/phases/4/closing: However you choose, someone is unhappy.
events/1300_priore/phases/5/title: Your Closest Friend Is On the List
events/1300_priore/phases/5/narrative: The pen hangs over the list. Under ringleaders of the Whites: Guido Cavalcanti — the man who taught you to write poetry, your “first friend.”
events/1300_priore/phases/5/options/0/re: Then the order against the Blacks is void too — Corso stays in the city, and the blood on the Santa Trinita square was spilled for nothing. The city goes up in flames.
events/1300_priore/phases/5/options/1/te: Sign. The same rule for everyone.
events/1300_priore/phases/5/options/1/re:
(quietly) Guido, forgive me.
The city comes before the man.
events/1300_priore/phases/5/conclusion/n: Cavalcanti was sent to Sarzana, where the swamp air was full of fever. He caught malaria; he was allowed home, and died that August. Years later, in Inferno X, Dante meets his father — the old man sits up out of a burning tomb: “Where is my son? Why is he not walking with you?” Dante hesitates for one moment, and the old man, thinking his son is dead, falls back into the tomb. Dante never got to finish the sentence.
events/1300_priore/phases/6/panels/0/dia: Dante the prior, bent over his desk. The candle flame wavers.
events/1300_priore/phases/6/panels/1/dia: The picture darkens. The papers on the desk slowly turn into vines and branches.
events/1300_priore/phases/6/panels/2/dia: Years later he picks up the pen and sets the story back in this year — the middle of his life, the year when nothing was lost yet and everything had already begun to go.

Nel mezzo del cammin di nostra vita —
Midway on the journey of our life, I found myself in a dark wood, for the right road was lost.
events/1300_priore/phases/7/prompt:
The first line of the Comedy is a man lost in a wood.
Use the pieces below to build one sentence: why does he start the book here?
events/1300_priore/phases/7/sentence: Because {s1}, {s2} — {s3}. So he made the first page of the book {s4}.
events/1300_priore/phases/7/tokens/0/tex: the city was torn in two by the two parties
events/1300_priore/phases/7/tokens/1/tex: he became a prior and, by the rule, exiled the leading men of both parties together
events/1300_priore/phases/7/tokens/2/tex: his close friend Guido was on the list and he signed anyway; Guido fell ill in exile and died soon after coming home
events/1300_priore/phases/7/tokens/3/tex: a man in a dark wood who cannot find the right road
events/1300_priore/phases/7/tokens/4/tex: he saw the pope in Rome in the Jubilee year
events/1300_priore/phases/7/tokens/5/tex: Florence's florin coin was used all over Europe
events/1300_priore/phases/7/canonical: Because the city was torn in two by the two parties, he became a prior and by the rule exiled the leading men of both parties together — his close friend Guido was on the list and he signed anyway; Guido fell ill in exile and died soon after coming home. So he made the first page of the book a man in a dark wood who cannot find the right road.
events/1300_priore/phases/7/note:
Two pieces are left over: the pope and the coin are both real, and both matter, but they are not on this chain of cause and effect.

“Lost” is not a figure of speech. He did the public thing right and destroyed his friend; two years later the same rule was used to destroy him. A man has to get that far before he says he is in the middle of a wood and cannot find the road.
events/1300_priore/phases/8/transitionTe:
There is light on the hilltop. Three beasts block the road.
This is page one of the Comedy — and what it describes is himself, in 1300.
events/1300_priore/phases/8/announcement: Boccaccio: “In the real 1300 he signed his closest friend onto an exile list. In the invented 1300 he is lost in a dark wood. My friends — these two are the same thing.”
quiz/1300_priore/quizzes/0/question: In which year did Dante set the story of the Divine Comedy?
quiz/1300_priore/quizzes/0/options/1: 1300 (the year he was a prior, the middle of his life)
quiz/1300_priore/quizzes/0/explanation: The Comedy is set in Easter week, 1300 — “midway on the journey of our life,” age thirty-five. That is exactly the year he became a prior in real life, the year everything was about to turn: nothing lost yet, and everything already beginning to go.
quiz/1300_priore/quizzes/1/question: In 1300, while Dante was a prior, which close friend did he exile to stop the party fighting?
quiz/1300_priore/quizzes/1/explanation: To stop the Whites and Blacks killing each other, and to keep “the same rule for everyone,” the priors exiled the ringleaders of both parties together — and on the Whites' list was Cavalcanti, Dante's “first friend.” He caught malaria in the fever country and died that August. Corso was the leader of the Blacks who was exiled.
quiz/1300_priore/quizzes/2/question:
Fill in the opening of the Inferno:
“Midway on the journey of our life, I found myself in a ___ wood”
quiz/1300_priore/quizzes/2/explanation: The opening of Inferno I: “Nel mezzo del cammin di nostra vita / mi ritrovai per una selva oscura” — Midway on the journey of our life, I found myself in a dark wood.
events/1308_inferno/phases/0/transitionT: At the lectern, Boccaccio reads a line Dante wrote about himself in the Convivio.
events/1308_inferno/phases/0/announcemen: “I am a ship with no sail and no rudder, blown by the dry wind of poverty to every port, river mouth and shore.” — Boccaccio: “The sixth year of exile. What you are about to see is a man sinking to the bottom, and then picking up his pen down there.”
events/1308_inferno/phases/1/narrative: Living off other people. Verona, the court of the Scala family — your patron's bread, the last seat at the table.
events/1308_inferno/phases/1/instruction: Walk about under the arcade. See what it is like to eat at another man's table.
events/1308_inferno/phases/1/npcs/0/dial: Signor Alighieri, at tonight's dinner you sit at the last place — down by the door.
No offence. Seats go by rank. And you these days… well.
events/1308_inferno/phases/1/npcs/1/dial: Everyone here has a use: I make my lord laugh, the cook fills him up, the soldiers keep him safe.
A poet? Ha! A poet is the fruit bowl after dinner — nobody notices if it isn't there.
events/1308_inferno/phases/1/npcs/2/dial: Alighieri! The brothers are gathering. We join the Ghibellines and fight our way back into Florence!
Your name is still on our roll. If you don't come, you're a traitor.
events/1308_inferno/phases/1/npcs/3/dial: Sir, don't listen to them. Tell me about Virgil — yesterday we got to Book VI, where Aeneas goes down to the world of the dead…
(The young lord of the Scala house, the only one at court who treats him as a teacher. Years later, the Paradiso will be dedicated to the grown-up Cangrande.)
events/1308_inferno/phases/2/narrative: The White envoy stands under the arcade, waiting for an answer. Fight your way home — is that the road home, or the road to death?
events/1308_inferno/phases/2/question: Fight your way home with the exiled Whites?
events/1308_inferno/phases/2/options/0/t: Go. Fight our way into Florence!
events/1308_inferno/phases/2/options/0/r: 20 July 1304, La Lastra. The army of the exiled Whites falls apart. Bodies everywhere. If you had been there, you would already be dead. — Think again.
events/1308_inferno/phases/2/options/1/r:
Your hatred and their hatred are the same thing.
Rather than walk with fools — I will be a party of one (parte per te stesso).
events/1308_inferno/phases/2/conclusion/: After the disaster at La Lastra in 1304, Dante broke with the exiled Whites for good, and from then on he was a party of one. He had lost his last side — and for the first time he was really free. A man with no party to speak for him can only speak to everyone.
events/1308_inferno/phases/3/sin/did:
In life they took money to see the future for other people: who would win, who would die, which day to send the army out.
Some believed it, some were frauds. Dante is putting them in Hell — and the punishment is his to decide.
events/1308_inferno/phases/3/question: If you were writing this part, what would you turn them into?
events/1308_inferno/phases/3/slots/1/lab: So forever after, they can only
events/1308_inferno/phases/3/parts/2/tex: Stuffed head-down into a crack in the rock
events/1308_inferno/phases/3/parts/3/tex: Turned into a stone statue that can't move
events/1308_inferno/phases/3/parts/6/tex: walk the same road ten thousand times
events/1308_inferno/phases/3/danteVersio:
Their heads are twisted around backwards, their faces looking at their own spines. To go forward they have to walk backwards — because they can never see what is in front of them again.
Their tears run down their backs. (Inferno XX)
events/1308_inferno/phases/3/mirror/sin: Alive: had to see what was ahead
events/1308_inferno/phases/3/mirror/puni: Dead: can only ever see behind
events/1308_inferno/phases/3/rule:
Turn the shape of the sin over, and you have the shape of the punishment.
Dante gave this rule a name: contrapasso.

Once you see the rule, you can work out the other eight circles yourself — which is exactly what comes next.
events/1308_inferno/phases/4/transitionT:
The Inferno is being written canto by canto, and copied from court to court.
Late autumn 1308, a messenger bursts in under the arcade —
events/1308_inferno/phases/4/announcemen:
“Through me you go into the city of grief,
through me you go into pain that never ends,
through me you go among the people who are lost.

You who come in, leave every hope outside.”
events/1308_inferno/phases/4/dufu_reacti:
(head snaps up)
…Maybe there is still hope.
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/0/question: Which language did Dante decide to write the Divine Comedy in?
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/0/options/0: Latin — the proper language of scholars and the Church
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/0/options/1: French — the usual language of court literature
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/0/options/2: The Italian vernacular — “the language the woman in the bakery can read too”
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/0/options/3: Greek — the language of the ancient epics
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/0/explanation: In De vulgari eloquentia Dante defended his mother tongue, and he wrote the Comedy in the Tuscan vernacular — a decision that lifted the “vernacular” into a language for literature, and the reason he is called the “father of the Italian language.”
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/1/question: When Dante says he is “a party of one” (parte per te stesso), what does he mean?
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/1/options/0: He started a new political party
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/1/options/1: He refused to join the exiled Whites and the Ghibellines in fighting their way home, and broke with them
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/1/options/3: He swore loyalty to the Scala family
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/1/explanation: The exiled Whites teamed up with the Ghibellines to fight their way home, and were crushed at La Lastra in 1304. Dante refused to take part and broke with them — a party of one. After that he belonged to no side, and spoke to everyone instead.
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/2/question:
Inferno III, the last line of the writing over the gate of Hell:
“You who enter here, abandon all ___”
quiz/1308_inferno/quizzes/2/explanation: “Lasciate ogne speranza, voi ch'intrate” — you who enter here, abandon all hope. Dante cut the deepest despair of his exile into the gate of the Inferno; then he pushed it open, went in, and began to write.
events/1313_impero/phases/0/transitionTe: At the lectern, Boccaccio unrolls copies of three letters.
events/1313_impero/phases/0/announcement: Boccaccio: “The last political gamble of his life. He put everything he had — including any chance of going home — on one German. Watch how he places the bet.”
events/1313_impero/phases/1/narrative: Henry VII leads his army over the Alps. On the exile’s desk three open letters are written, one after another, and left lying there.
events/1313_impero/phases/1/instruction: Read all three letters, then hear what the scribe says.
events/1313_impero/phases/1/npcs/0/name: Letter 1 · To the princes of Italy
events/1313_impero/phases/1/npcs/0/dialo: To the Kings and Princes of Italy
“Look, now is the time of grace! The bridegroom is coming. Bride of Italy, dry your tears — the Emperor of Rome comes to bring peace to all peoples!”
events/1313_impero/phases/1/npcs/1/dialo: “You fools! You trample every law of God and man, greed drives you to every kind of wrong — your walls will not save you. Under the eagle you will tremble!”
(the pen does not stop) That felt good. It also nails me to the exile list for good.
events/1313_impero/phases/1/npcs/2/dialo: “Why do you delay? You winter in Milan and think Tuscany is nothing to worry about? Wrong! Strike Florence first — that viper, that sick sheep, poisoning the whole flock!”
events/1313_impero/phases/1/npcs/3/dialo: (his hand shaking) Sir, these letters… the city you are cursing is your own.
Once they go out and every city has read them — Florence will never, never pardon you.
events/1313_impero/phases/2/narrative: The scribe holds the letters and waits for the last word.
events/1313_impero/phases/2/question: Do the three letters go out?
events/1313_impero/phases/2/options/0/re: He did not wait. History does not offer that option — the man in front of you never left himself a way back.
events/1313_impero/phases/2/options/1/re:
Justice turns on this one throw.
Send them — let all Italy hear.
events/1313_impero/phases/2/conclusion/n: The three letters travel all over Italy. Florence answers by shutting Dante out of every pardon, for ever. He staked the road home on a dream of empire.
events/1313_impero/phases/3/travelNarrat: Henry VII crosses the Alps and comes south. Stop by stop, the fever cools.
events/1313_impero/phases/3/instruction: Follow the eagle’s route. Click each stop.
events/1313_impero/phases/3/waypoints/0/: In Sant’Ambrogio, Henry puts on the iron crown of Lombardy. In the watching crowd an exiled poet pushes to the front — bends down, and kisses the Emperor’s feet.
I saw him. Justice in the flesh, alive. Twenty years — and this is the first time I have felt so close to home.
events/1313_impero/phases/3/waypoints/1/: Brescia shuts its gates and holds out. Four months of siege, disease everywhere, and the allied army begins to fall apart. The Guelf cities watch coldly — King Robert of Naples is already gathering troops.
events/1313_impero/phases/3/waypoints/2/: Street fighting in Rome. The enemy holds St Peter’s, so the crowning has to move to the Lateran — half a coronation. The Pope is far away in Avignon, and even his envoys are just going through the motions.
The crown is on, but the doors of St Peter’s are shut. …A bad sign.
events/1313_impero/phases/3/waypoints/3/: The army marches south again. On 24 August, in a small town near Siena called Buonconvento —
events/1313_impero/phases/4/transitionTe:
Before the bier, the eagle banner is furled.
After Henry died, Dante never hoped for anything from the politics of this world again.
He wrote the Emperor into the Paradiso.

At the lectern, Boccaccio is quiet for a long time.
events/1313_impero/phases/4/announcement: Boccaccio: “He lost the bet. But listen — it was because the throne on earth stood empty that he built the whole of Heaven into a courtroom. The verdicts of the Divine Comedy last longer than any emperor’s.”
quiz/1313_impero/quizzes/0/question: In 1310–1313, who did Dante stake his last political hopes on?
quiz/1313_impero/quizzes/0/options/2: Henry VII, the Holy Roman Emperor
quiz/1313_impero/quizzes/0/explanation: When Henry VII came south into Italy, Dante wrote open letter after open letter: telling the princes to go and meet him, cursing Florence, pushing Henry to attack Florence first — so savagely that he destroyed any chance of ever being pardoned. In 1313 Henry fell ill and died at Buonconvento, and the dream was over.
quiz/1313_impero/quizzes/1/question: What image did Dante use against the Church’s “sun and moon” argument, to say that empire and Church stand side by side?
quiz/1313_impero/quizzes/1/explanation: The Church taught the “sun and moon” doctrine: imperial power is the moon, and can only borrow its light from the papal sun. Dante answered with “two suns” (the image is in Purgatorio XVI): empire and Church each take their authority straight from God. The Monarchia argues the whole case; the Church later banned it and burned it.
quiz/1313_impero/quizzes/2/question:
Paradiso XXX, among the seats of the highest rose:
“One chair stands empty, with a ___ laid on it, waiting for the great Henry”
quiz/1313_impero/quizzes/2/explanation: Paradiso XXX: Beatrice points out to Dante the empty seat and the crown in the rose of Heaven — the emperor earth had no room for has a place kept for him there.
events/1315_amnistia/phases/0/narrative: The thirteenth year of exile. Florence declares an amnesty — and a letter arrives in the little courtyard where he lodges. Dante is almost fifty. He has missed home for thirteen years.
events/1315_amnistia/phases/0/instructio: Read the terms of the amnesty, then hear what the people around him say.
events/1315_amnistia/phases/0/npcs/0/dia: Master Alighieri, good news! The city is pardoning its exiles. Let me read you the terms —
“One: pay a fine. Two: put on the penitent's robe and the paper hat. Three: walk with the procession to the Baptistery of San Giovanni, and make an offering to the patron saint for your sins.”
Walk it once, and you can go home. Sir, plenty of men beg for this and never get it.
events/1315_amnistia/phases/0/npcs/1/dia: On the parchment, the commune's seal he knows so well. The words “penance” and “offering” are written out especially neatly.
The Baptistery of San Giovanni… where I was baptized. They want me walked through the streets as a sinner, back to the place my life began.
events/1315_amnistia/phases/0/npcs/2/dia: Sir, Grandpa says you look south every single day.
What's over there, in the south?
events/1315_amnistia/phases/0/npcs/3/dia: Father. The sentence takes in your sons as well — Jacopo and I are on the exile list too.
Just take it. The paper hat comes off after one day. I want to go home.
events/1315_amnistia/phases/1/situation:
Thirteen years on, a letter from Florence:
pay the fine, wear the penitent's robe, be marched through the streets confessing — and they will let you back.
events/1315_amnistia/phases/1/options/0/: Accept. Pay the fine, walk in the procession, go home — his wife and children again, and his own city to grow old in.
events/1315_amnistia/phases/1/options/1/: Refuse. Rather grow old and die under someone else's roof.
events/1315_amnistia/phases/1/sameNote: You guessed it. So here's the next question: what made him think that was worth it?
events/1315_amnistia/phases/1/diffNote: He didn't take it. Thirteen years, one chance to go home, and he didn't take it.
events/1315_amnistia/phases/1/reveal:
“This is not the road home for me.
If there is another road that costs Dante nothing in honor and dignity, I will walk it without a moment's hesitation.
If there is not — then I will never set foot in Florence.

Can I not see the sun and the moon and the stars anywhere else?
Can I not think the sweetest thoughts unless I first shame myself in front of my own city?
Bread, I will not go short of, anywhere.”
— Letter XII
events/1315_amnistia/phases/1/consequenc:
A few months later Florence changed the sentence: Dante and his sons, beheading. (Before that it was burning.)

He never went back. He died in Ravenna in 1321 and was buried there.
For six hundred years afterwards Florence asked Ravenna for his bones, again and again, and never once got them.
The tomb built for him in the church of Santa Croce is empty to this day.
events/1315_amnistia/phases/2/transition:
A few months later Florence changed the sentence:
Dante and his sons, beheading.
(Before that it was burning.)
events/1315_amnistia/phases/2/announceme: Boccaccio closes his lecture notes and says nothing for a long moment: “Fellow Florentines. Our city shut its best son out twice — the first time with fire, the second time with a paper hat. And he answered with a whole Paradiso: there is only one crowning he will take. If the Divine Comedy ever brings him home, he will stand at the font where he was baptized and put on the laurel.”
events/1315_amnistia/phases/2/dufu_react:
“If this holy poem can beat the cruelty that shuts me out of the sheepfold —
I will come back with another voice, in another fleece,
and at the font where I was baptized I will take the laurel.” (Paradiso XXV)
quiz/1315_amnistia/quizzes/0/question: In the 1315 amnesty, what did Florence ask an exile to do in exchange for coming home?
quiz/1315_amnistia/quizzes/0/options/0: Swear loyalty to the Blacks' government
quiz/1315_amnistia/quizzes/0/options/1: Pay a fine, walk in the procession in a penitent's robe and paper hat, and make an offering at the Baptistery
quiz/1315_amnistia/quizzes/0/options/2: Hand over everything he had written
quiz/1315_amnistia/quizzes/0/options/3: Serve three years in the army
quiz/1315_amnistia/quizzes/0/explanation: The terms were: pay a fine, put on the penitent's robe and paper hat, walk with the procession to the Baptistery of San Giovanni and “make an offering” — humiliated in public, as a sinner. Dante's answer, in Letter XII: “This is not the road home for me.”
quiz/1315_amnistia/quizzes/1/question: After Dante refused the amnesty, what did Florence change his sentence to?
quiz/1315_amnistia/quizzes/1/options/2: Beheading for Dante and his sons (before that it was burning)
quiz/1315_amnistia/quizzes/1/explanation: A few months after he refused, Florence changed the sentence to beheading for Dante and his sons — his sons were pulled in with him. He had already written his answer in the letter that turned it down: “Bread, I will not go short of, anywhere.”
quiz/1315_amnistia/quizzes/2/question:
At the start of Paradiso XXV, Dante writes down the only crowning he will accept:
“I will come back with another voice, in another fleece, and at the font where I was baptized I will take the ___”
quiz/1315_amnistia/quizzes/2/explanation: Paradiso XXV: “If this holy poem can beat the cruelty that shuts me out of the sheepfold… I will take the laurel at the font where I was baptized.” That font is the Baptistery of San Giovanni, where he was baptized in 1265 — he died still waiting for it, and Florence owes him that laurel to this day.
events/1321_ravenna/phases/0/transitionT:
The church of Santo Stefano. Twice as many candles lit as usual.
Boccaccio opens the last volume of his notes.
events/1321_ravenna/phases/0/announcemen: Boccaccio: “The story has reached its end. A city by the sea took him in — Ravenna. You are about to see how a man who had lost everything finished writing everything.”
events/1321_ravenna/phases/1/narrative: Around 1318 the lord of Ravenna, Guido Novello da Polenta, sends messengers to invite him. The sea pines rustle, his children come to join him — the last stop of the exile, and it feels like a home.
events/1321_ravenna/phases/1/instruction: Walk between the pines and the court. Meet the people here.
events/1321_ravenna/phases/1/npcs/0/dial: That you would come is Ravenna's good fortune, master. The house is ready and the pay is generous — no. Not a retainer. A master.
I write verse too. Some day… would you look at mine and correct it? (The lord bows like a pupil.)
events/1321_ravenna/phases/1/npcs/1/dial: Father. I have taken vows at the convent of Santo Stefano here in the city.
My name in religion is — Sister Beatrice.
events/1321_ravenna/phases/1/npcs/2/dial: Copies of the Inferno and the Purgatorio are passing from city to city. Master — the Paradiso is still a few cantos short.
Finish it. All Italy is waiting.
events/1321_ravenna/phases/2/narrative: The church of Sant'Apollinare. Gold mosaics from the sixth century, burning for eight hundred years.
events/1321_ravenna/phases/2/instruction: Click the things in the church that move him.
events/1321_ravenna/phases/2/npcs/0/dial: The gold tiles flicker on and off in the candlelight, like a sea of light gone solid. The saints stand in a gold that never ends.
A gold vault… so the light of Heaven has been seen on earth after all.
(The whirlpools of light, the rose of light, the river of light in the Paradiso — the first sketch of all of it is on a ceiling in Ravenna.)
events/1321_ravenna/phases/2/npcs/1/dial: A letter comes from Giovanni del Virgilio, a scholar in Bologna: “What a waste, to write a lasting work in the common tongue. Write it again in Latin, and I will get you the laurel crown in Bologna.”
(He picks up his pen and sends back two country poems in Latin verse — faultless craft, and the answer is one word: no.)
The girl in the bakery cannot read Latin. The common tongue is thirteen cantos away from winning.
events/1321_ravenna/phases/3/transitionT:
Summer 1321. Ravenna and Venice fall into a quarrel.
Dante goes to Venice as Guido's envoy to settle it, and comes back through the marsh channels —
mosquitoes, fever. Malaria.
events/1321_ravenna/phases/3/announcemen: Dante Alighieri dies in Ravenna, fifty-six years old. His children are at the bedside. The last thirteen cantos of the Paradiso — they search the whole study, and no one finds them.
events/1321_ravenna/phases/3/dufu_reacti:
Bread will not fail me anywhere…
Only the Paradiso… thirteen cantos short.
events/1321_ravenna/phases/4/narrative: Eight months later. A story people still tell —
events/1321_ravenna/phases/4/panels/0/di: His son Jacopo sees his father in a dream. White robe, smiling, light all around him.
events/1321_ravenna/phases/4/panels/1/di: “What you are looking for,” his father lifts a hand and points at the wall of his old bedroom, “is there.”
events/1321_ravenna/phases/4/panels/2/di: They pull back the wall hanging — there is a small niche in the wall, and inside it a damp, mouldy stack of manuscript.
events/1321_ravenna/phases/4/panels/3/di: They brush off the mould. The writing can still be read — the last thirteen cantos of the Paradiso.
events/1321_ravenna/phases/4/panels/4/di:
l'amor che move il sole e l'altre stelle —
It is love that moves the sun and the stars.
events/1321_ravenna/phases/5/rule: Dante's universe: the earth in the middle, nine heavens wrapped around it. The further out, the faster it turns — because it is closer to God.
events/1321_ravenna/phases/5/spheres/0/h: People who could not keep a vow
events/1321_ravenna/phases/5/spheres/0/n: Piccarda is here. Her own brother dragged her out of the convent and forced her to marry — someone else broke the vow for her, and still she can go no higher than the lowest ring. She says: here I am content.
events/1321_ravenna/phases/5/spheres/1/h: People who did good, and wanted the credit too
events/1321_ravenna/phases/5/spheres/1/n: The emperor Justinian is here, speaking up for Roman law. Mix a little wish for fame into your good deeds and you cannot climb higher than this.
